title: Introduction to Harmony and Intervals
theoryMarkdown:
Chapter 1: Introduction to Harmony and Intervals

Introduction to Harmony

Harmony is a fundamental pillar in music, since it not only gives structure to compositions, but also evokes emotions and connects listeners with the work.

The objectives of this book are:

  • Provide a solid understanding of the principles of harmony.
  • Develop skills to analyze, compose and improvise music effectively.
  • Promote musical creativity through the practical application of theory.

The importance of harmony lies in its ability to create sound contexts that accompany the melody, providing richness and depth to the music. Throughout this book, we will learn to identify, construct and apply harmonic concepts that will help us turn our musical ideas into reality.

Intervals - The Basic Unit

Intervals are the basis of harmony and represent the distance between two notes. They are divided into:

  • Melodic Range: It is when you play one note and then the other.
  • Harmonic Interval: It is when 2 notes are played at the same time.

Interval Table (From C)

Distance Interval (Semitones) Example from C
1 semitone Minor second C a C#
2 semitones Second major C a D
3 semitones minor third C a D#
4 semitones Major third C a E
5 semitones Fair fourth C a F
6 semitones Augmented fourth/diminished fifth C a F#
7 semitones fair fifth C a G
8 semitones Minor sixth/augmented fifth C a G#
9 semitones major sixth C a A
10 semitones minor seventh C a A#
11 semitones major seventh C a B
12 semitones Octave C a C (Octava)

Identification and Construction

ID: To identify an interval, it is essential to know the notes involved and count the distance in tones and semitones. Example: The interval of a major third is made up of four semitones. If we start on the note C (Do), the major third interval would be And (Mi).

Construction: To construct an interval, you must start with a base note and count up or down the number of tones and semitones required. Example: To construct a fair fifth from C (Do), we count seven semitones, which leads us to G (Sol).

title: Construction of Triad Chords
theoryMarkdown:
Chapter 2: Construction of Triad Chords

Introduction to Triads

Triad chords are the fundamental basis of harmony in music. They are made up of three notes and are classified into four main types: major, minor, diminished and augmented. Each type of chord is built from a root note, adding different intervals.

Major Chords

Construction: It is formed using the first (tonic), major third and perfect fifth of the scale.

C Major Chord Example: C (Do) - E (Mi) - G (Sol)

Minor Chords

Construction: It is formed using the first (tonic), minor third and perfect fifth of the scale.

C Minor Chord Example: C (Do) - Eb (My Flat) - G (Sol)

Diminished Chords

Construction: It is formed using the first (tonic), minor third and diminished fifth (which is a semitone below the perfect fifth).

Example Chord C Diminished: C (C) - Eb (E flat) - Gb (G flat)

Augmented Chords

Construction: It is formed using the first (tonic), major third and augmented fifth (a semitone above the perfect fifth).

Augmented C Chord Example: C (Do) - E (Mi) - G (Sol sustained)

visualizerTriggers.description: Render C, Cm, Cdim, Caug on strings 5, 4 and 3.

quiz.question: If you are playing a G Major (G - B - D) and you change the major third (B) to a minor third (Bb), what triad are you making?
quiz.explanation: Correct. By lowering the major third a semitone, it becomes a minor third, forming the G Minor triad.

quiz.question: You have a chord with the structure 1 - b3 - b5. If you raise the fifth a semitone (to a perfect 5th), what kind of triad does it become?
quiz.explanation: Correct. 1 - b3 - 5 is the formula for a Minor Triad.

quiz.question: The difference between a major triad and an augmented triad lies in the alteration of a single interval. Which is it?
quiz.explanation: Correct. The augmented triad is formed by raising the perfect fifth (5) to the augmented fifth (#5).

quiz.question: If you play the notes A - C - E, you are forming an A minor triad. Which note should you alter to transform it into a diminished triad?
quiz.explanation: Correct. To make it diminished, you must lower the perfect fifth (E) to the diminished fifth (Eb).

quiz.question: Knowing that an augmented chord is formed with the Tonic, Major 3rd and Augmented 5th, what notes make up the Augmented F triad (Faug)?
quiz.explanation: Correct. F is the tonic, A is the Major 3rd and C# is the Augmented 5th.

title: Major Scale and its Interval Structure
theoryMarkdown:
Chapter 3: Major Scale and its Interval Structure

Interval Structure of the Major Scale

The major scale is one of the fundamental foundations of music theory and the mother of our Western tonal music. It has a specific intervallic structure from its tonic.

  • Intervalic Formula: Tonic(1) - Major 2nd(2) - Major 3rd(3) - Just 4th(4) - Just 5th(5) - Major 6th(6) - Major 7th(7).
  • Pattern of Tones(T) and Semitones(S): T - T - S - T - T - T - S.

The C Major Scale and its Importance

The C major scale is unique because it contains no accidentals (neither sharps nor flats). It is composed of the sequence of natural notes: C - D - E - F - G - A - B - C.

🎸 View and Play Full Scale

This scale serves as a model and starting point for building all other major scales and understanding fundamental harmony. Its simplicity makes it ideal to begin harmonic study.

Harmonization of the C Major Scale

Harmonization involves building chords from each note of the major scale (using only the diatonic notes). By applying this in the C Major scale we obtain the following progression of triads:

  • 1. C Major (C - E - G)
  • 2. D Minor (D - F - A)
  • 3. And Minor (E - G - B)
  • 4. F Major (F - A - C)
  • 5. G Major (G - B - D)
  • 6. The Minor (A - C - E)
  • 7. B Diminished (B - D - F)

Case Study: Analysis of 'Let It Be' (The Beatles)

To understand the power of the Major Scale, let's analyze the verse of one of the great pop classics. This song is in the key of C Major (C) and exclusively uses chords from its harmonization (diatonic triads). It is the perfect example to hear how grades I, V, vi and IV interact.

▶️ Listen to Progression ⏹️ Stop
C [I] Tonic
G [V] Dominante
Am [vi] Relative Minor
F [IV] Subdominante
C [I] Tonic
G [V] Dominante
F [IV] Subdominante
C [I] Tonic

You will notice how the song starts from the absolute stability of the Tonic (I), generates tension by moving to the Dominant (V), makes a small melancholic detour towards its relative minor (vi) and lands softly on the Subdominant (IV). This I - V - vi - IV progression is the skeleton of thousands of world hits.

Scales with Sharps (#)

The concept is organized through the Circle of Fifths, which allows us to determine which notes are altered in each new major scale. The process consists of taking the perfect fifth of the tonic of the previous scale. Each new scale adds a sharp in the seventh degree.

Scales with Flats (b)

They are organized following the same principle but in the opposite direction (Circle of Fourths), generating descending alterations. In this case, the new keys are built by adding flats starting from the fourth degree of the previous scale.

Transposition: Changing Key with Tables

The magic of thinking in Roman degrees (I, V, vi, IV) instead of fixed chords is that you can move any song to the key that best suits your voice. You just have to look for the new key in the tables above and copy the chords from those same columns. Let's see how 'Let It Be' looks if we transpose it to A Flat Major (Ab) and E Major (E).

C#m [vi] Relative Minor

quiz.question: What is the perfect 5th of C that begins the sharp circle?
quiz.explanation: The perfect fifth of C is G, which marks the first scale with a sharp in the key signature.

quiz.question: In the key of D Major, what is the chord of the VI degree?
quiz.explanation: The sixth degree of D Major generates a minor chord, in this case B minor (Bm), which is also its relative minor.

quiz.question: What note is altered (sharp) when going from C Major to G Major?
quiz.explanation: When moving to the key of G Major, the seventh degree becomes sensitive, introducing the alteration F#.

quiz.question: What is the diatonic chord of the VII degree in the A Major scale?
quiz.explanation: The VII degree of a major scale is a diminished chord. In A Major, the seventh degree is G sharp (G#), forming G#dim.

quiz.question: What major scale has exactly 4 sharps in its key signature?
quiz.explanation: Following the circle of fifths: G (1), D (2), A (3), E (4). E Major has 4 sharps: F#, C#, G#, D#.

title: Construction of Tetrad Chords
theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 4: Construction of Tetrad Chords ## 1. Tetrad Chords

Tetrad Chords and Their Formation

Tetrad chords, or seventh chords, are made up of four distinctive notes. They are fundamental in musical genres such as jazz, blues, bossa nova or neo-soul, since they add greater harmonic richness, tension and color.

Just as triads are formed by overlapping thirds, tetrads add an additional third over the fifth of the original triad, generating a seventh interval from the root note.

  • Major 7 Chord (Maj7): Major Triad + Major Seventh. Formula: 1 - 3 - 5 - 7. Example: Cmaj7.
  • Dominant Chord (7): Major Triad + Minor Seventh. Formula: 1 - 3 - 5 - b7. Example: C7.
  • Minor 7 chord (m7): Minor Triad + Minor Seventh. Formula: 1 - b3 - 5 - b7. Example: Cm7.
  • Minor Chord with Major Seventh (m(maj7)): Minor Triad + Major Seventh. Formula: 1 - b3 - 5 - 7. Example: Cm(7M).
  • Semi-diminished chord (m7b5): Diminished Triad + Minor Seventh. Formula: 1 - b3 - b5 - b7. Example: Cm7(5b).
  • Diminished Chord (dim7): Diminished Triad + Diminished Seventh. Formula: 1 - b3 - b5 - bb7. Example: Cdim7.

Application in Harmonic Progressions

Tetrads enrich harmonic movement, as we can see in the famous progressions II - V - I, extending what we saw previously with triads.

  • II - V - I in major key: It is structured using the corresponding degrees of the scale: the II degree is minor 7, the V degree is dominant, and the I degree is Major 7. Example in C major: Dm7 - G7 - Cmaj7.
  • II - V - I in a minor key: The concept is similar but using the degrees of the harmonic minor scale: the II degree is semi-diminished, the V degree is dominant (to create tension towards the tonic), and the I degree is minor 7. Example in A minor: Bm7b5 - E7 - Am7.
  • Blues Cadence: A characteristic blues progression using dominant seventh chords. Example in C: C7 - F7 - G7.

Tetrad Chord Charts (Sharps and Flats)

🎧 Practical Application: Case Study

Theory comes to life when we apply it. To master the sonority of tetrad chords (Maj7, m7 and dominant 7), the standard "Mack the Knife" It is the perfect laboratory. Its harmonic progression allows us to clearly hear how the seventh adds color, depth and movement to each chord within the same key.

🎵 Analyze Mack the Knife in the Player

quiz.question: What note is added to a triad to make it a tetrad?
quiz.explanation: Tetrads are formed by adding a third to the triad, which results in a seventh interval from the root.

quiz.question: What is the formula for the Maj7 chord?
quiz.explanation: The Maj7 chord consists of a major triad plus a major seventh.

quiz.question: In the key of C, what is the m7 chord that corresponds to degree II?
quiz.explanation: In C major, the II degree is D, and its diatonic seventh chord is Dm7.

quiz.question: What type of seventh chord is formed in the V degree of a major scale?
quiz.explanation: The V degree of a major scale naturally forms a dominant seventh chord (7).

quiz.question: What is the VII degree chord in the G major scale using tetrads?
quiz.explanation: In G major, the VII degree is F#, and it forms a semi-diminished chord (m7b5).

title: Arpeggios and Harmonic Functions
theoryMarkdown:
Chapter 5: Arpeggios and Harmonic Functions

1. What is an Arpeggio?

Unlike a classic chord where we structure the hand to sound all the notes in unison (Stack / Block), a arpeggio It consists of playing the notes that make up the chord sequentially, one after another.

Arpeggios are essential for bassists and lead guitarists, as they allow harmony to be outlined while creating melodic movement. Mastering arpeggios is the first step to fluid improvisation and creating dynamic bass lines (Walking Bass).

2. Triad Arpeggios

We can construct sequences of three (or four, counting the eighth) notes based on the different qualities.

  • ● Major Triad: Formed by Tonic, 3rd Major and 5th Justa. View the route of C Major.
  • ● Minor Triad: Formed by Tonic, minor 3rd and Just 5th. Visualize the melodic jump of The Minor.
  • ● Diminished Triad: Formed by Tonic, minor 3rd and diminished 5th. It has a strong resolving tension. Visualize B Diminished (We will show the frequently used dim7 tetrad).

3. Tetrad Arpeggios

By adding the seventh, the arpeggio consists of 4 notes before repeating the eighth, opening the almost perfect 4/4 time signature if we play with quarter notes.

  • ● Arpeggio Maj7: Tonic, Major 3rd, Just 5th, Major 7th. Produces an open and bright melodic contour. View the arpeggio Cmaj7.
  • ● Arpeggio m7: Tonic, minor 3rd, Just 5th, minor 7th. Frequent in smooth jazz or funk accompaniment lines. Visualize Am7.
  • ● Dominant Arpeggio (7): Tonic, Major 3rd, Just 5th, Minor 7th. Fundamental pillar in blues, indicating directionality. View the classic G7.
  • ● Semi-diminished arpeggio (m7b5): Tonic, minor 3rd, diminished 5th, minor 7th. Fundamental for Grade VII of the major scale. Visualize Bm7b5.
  • ● Diminished Arpeggio (dim7): Tonic, minor 3rd, diminished 5th, diminished 7th. Symmetrical arpeggio, full of tension. Visualize Bdim7.

4. Principal and Substitute Harmonic Functions

In the major key (e.g. C Major), each chord plays a role or harmonic function:

  • ● Tonic (I): Stability, rest.
  • ● Subdominante (IV): Medium tension, movement.
  • ● Dominante (V): Maximum tension, need to resolve to the tonic.

Main Harmonic Functions:

  • ● Cmaj7 (I): C - E - G - B
  • ● Fmaj7 (IV): F - A - C - E
  • ● G7 (V): G - B - D - F

Substitute Harmonic Functions:

Chords that share 3 notes with the main ones can function as substitutes.

  • ● Em7 (III) y Am7 (VI) can replace Cmaj7. (Note how the Am7 share A - C - E - G; 3 notes out of 4).
  • ● Dm7 (II) can replace Fmaj7.
  • ● Bm7♭5 (VII) can replace G7.

Basic progression in C major:

Cmaj7 -> Fmaj7 -> G7 -> Resolution: Cmaj7

Progression with substitute functions:

Replacing the initial Cmaj7, the Fmaj7 and modifying the Dominant:

Am7 -> Dm7 -> Bm7b5 -> Resolution: Cmaj7

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a chord and an arpeggio?
quiz.explanation: An arpeggio breaks down the chord, playing its notes one after another (sequentially) rather than simultaneously.

quiz.question: What notes make up the arpeggio of a major triad?
quiz.explanation: The major triad always consists of the Tonic, the major 3rd and the perfect 5th.

quiz.question: In a diminished triad arpeggio, what is the fifth like?
quiz.explanation: The main feature of the 'diminished' is the flat fifth (5b) combined with the minor third.

quiz.question: When converting a triad arpeggio to a tetrad arpeggio, what note are we adding?
quiz.explanation: The tetrad is composed by adding a seventh to the base triad.

quiz.question: What are arpeggios mainly used for in music?
options: Para resaltar notas importantes y crear líneas melódicas fluidas
quiz.explanation: Arpeggios harmonically connect a section, providing melody and reinforcing the target notes of each harmonic passage.

title: Inversions and Modes of the Major Scale
theoryMarkdown:
Chapter 6: Inversions and Modes of the Major Scale

In this chapter we will explore chord inversions and how they smooth out harmonic progressions.

1. Triad Inversions

A triad has three arrangements depending on the note that is placed on the bass:

  • ● Fundamental State: The tone in the bass. Example: C (C - E - G).
  • ● First Investment: The 3rd on the bass. Example: C/E (E - G - C).
    Voice Structure:
    Low: E (Mi)
    ➔
    G (Sol)
    ➔
    C (Do)
  • ● Second Investment: The 5th on the bass. Example: C/G (G - C - E).
    Voice Structure:
    Low: G (Sol)
    ➔
    C (Do)
    ➔
    E (Mi)

2. Tetrad Reversals

Tetrads (seventh chords) have four arrangements:

  • ● Fundamental State: Tonic in the bass. Example: Cmaj7 (C - E - G - B).
  • ● First Investment: 3rd on the bass. Example: Cmaj7/E (E - G - B - C).
    Voice Structure:
    Low: E (Mi)
    ➔
    G (Sol)
    ➔
    B (And)
    ➔
    C (Do)
  • ● Second Investment: 5th on the bass. Example: Cmaj7/G (G - B - C - E).
    Voice Structure:
    Low: G (Sol)
    ➔
    B (And)
    ➔
    C (Do)
    ➔
    E (Mi)
  • ● Third Investment: 7th on the bass. Example: Cmaj7/B (B - C - E - G).
    Voice Structure:
    Low: B (And)
    ➔
    C (Do)
    ➔
    E (Mi)
    ➔
    G (Sol)

3. How Loudness Affects Progressions

The movement of chords in the fundamental state usually has large jumps in the bass. Inversions allow for joint bass lines.

Progression with Jumps (Fundamental State):

C -> G -> Am -> F

Smooth Progression with Inversions:

Using inversions to create a descending bass line step by step, giving continuity and smoothness to the harmonic flow.

C -> G/B -> Am -> F/A

4. Introduction to Greek Modes

The Greek modes are different perspectives of the same scale. If we take the notes of the major scale (for example, C Major: C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and start playing them from different degrees, we get different interval structures, each with a unique "color" or "character." These are the 7 modes:

1. Ionian (Major Scale)

Grade and Notes: From 1st grade | Notes: C-D-E-F-G-A-B

T - 2M - 3M - 4J - 5J - 6M - 7M

Character: Bright, cheerful, stable sound. It is the basis of our traditional harmony.

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"Let It Be" (The Beatles) / "La Bamba" (Ritchie Valens)

2. Doric

Grade and Notes: From 2nd grade | Notes: D-E-F-G-A-B-C

T - 2M - 3M - 4J - 5J - 6M - 7M

Character: Minor, but with a bright and "jazzy" touch thanks to its major sixth.

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"So What" (Miles Davis) / "Oye Como Va" (Santana) / "Get Lucky" (Daft Punk)

3. Phrygian

Grade and Notes: From 3rd grade | Notes: E-F-G-A-B-C-D

T - 2m - 3m - 4J - 5J - 6m - 7m

Character: Dark, exotic flavor, flamenco style or dark metal (for its second minor).

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"Asturias" (Isaac Albéniz) / "Symphony of Destruction" (Megadeth)

4. Lydia

Grade and Notes: From 4th grade | Notes: F-G-A-B-C-D-E

T - 2M - 3M - 4A - 5J - 6M - 7M

Character: Major, dreamy, magical or spatial by its augmented fourth (#4).

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"The Simpsons Theme" (Danny Elfman) / "Flying in a Blue Dream" (Joe Satriani)

5. Mixolidio

Grade and Notes: From 5th grade | Notes: G-A-B-C-D-E-F

T - 2M - 3M - 4J - 5J - 6M - 7M

Character: Major, bluesy, classic rock. It sounds like road and summer because of its minor seventh.

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"Sweet Home Alabama" (Lynyrd Skynyrd) / "Highway to Hell" (AC/DC)

6. Aeolian (Minor Natural)

Grade and Notes: From 6th grade | Notes: A-B-C-D-E-F-G

T - 2m - 3m - 4J - 5J - 6m - 7m

Character: Typically sad, melancholic, epic. It is the standard minor scale.

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"Losing My Religion" (R.E.M.) / "Smells Like Teen Spirit" (Nirvana)

7. Locrian

Grade and Notes: From 7th grade | Notes: B-C-D-E-F-G-A

T - 2m - 3m - 4J - 5d - 6m - 7m

Character: Very unstable, tense and dark (due to its diminished 5th in addition to the minor 2nd and 3rd).

See and Hear Scale

🎧 Hear it in action:

"Army of Me" (Björk - bassline) / "Juicebox" (The Strokes)

title: Natural Minor Scale
theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 7: Natural Minor Scale

1. Introduction to the Natural Minor Scale

The Natural Minor Scale, also known as Wind Mode, is one of the pillars of Western music. Its sound is usually associated with emotions such as melancholy, sadness or the times, and it is the natural counterpart of the major scale.

2. Formation and Structure of the Natural Minor Scale

Unlike the major scale, the natural minor scale has a distinct interval structure, mainly characterized by its minor third, minor sixth, and minor seventh. Its complete formula is:

Tonic + 2nd + 3rd + 4th + 5th + 6th + 7th

If we apply this structure starting from the note The (A), we obtain the scale notes The Minor:

A - B - C - D - E - F - G
See and Hear Scale (A Minor)

3. Harmonization in Tetrad Chords

By superimposing diatonic thirds over each degree of the A Natural Minor scale, we obtain the following four-note chords (tetrads):

Grade Chord Type Chord (Ej. A Minor)
i7 Minor 7 Am7
iiø7 Semi-diminished Bm7(b5)
IIImaj7 Mayor 7 Cmaj7
iv7 Minor 7 Dm7
v7 Minor 7 Em7
May 7 Mayor 7 Fmaj7
VII7 Dominant 7 G7

4. Harmonic Analysis of the Dominant Function

Unlike the major scale, where the fifth degree is a strong dominant chord (V7), in the Natural Minor Scale the fifth degree is a minor chord: v7 (Em7 in the key of A Minor).

Este acorde carece de la "nota sensible" (la séptima mayor de la escala, que en A Menor sería G#, pero aquí tenemos G natural). Sin la tensión del tritono que empuja a resolver hacia la tónica, la progresión v7 -{">"} i7 feels weak harmonically.

"This aspect gives the Natural Minor Scale a more relaxed sonority, less oriented toward the strong resolution found in traditional major harmony."

5. Stabilization with V7 (The Harmonic Minor Scale)

To solve this lack of resolution, European classical music introduced a modification: raising the seventh degree by half a step (from G to G# in A Minor). This creates the Harmonic Minor Scale and transform the weak chord v7 (Em7) in a strong dominant V7 (E7).

Grade Chord Notes

Minor Scales with Sharps (#) and their Tetrad Chords

Minor Scales with Flats (b) and their Tetrad Chords

Main Harmonic Functions

Tonic

Contribute Stability and absolute rest. It is the tonal center of the progression.

Grades: Im7, Im(maj7)

Example in A minor:

Am7 On(maj7)

Subdominante

Generate a moderate tension and acts as a logical bridge to the Dominant.

Grade: IVm7

Example in A minor:

Dm7

Dominant

Create a strong tension (due to the tritone) that requires mandatory resolution towards the Tonic.

Grade: V7

Example in A minor:

E7

Substitute Harmonic Functions

Tonic Substitutes

They share common notes with the I chord, maintaining the feeling of repose.

IIImaj7: Cmaj7

Subdominant Substitutes

They provide preparation and harmonic variety before the cadence.

IIm7(b5): Bm7(b5)
May 7: Fmaj7
VII7: G7

Dominant Substitutes

They maintain the strain of the tritone that forces us to resolve.

VII°7: G#°7

6. Case Study: Autumn Leaves and the engine of Jazz (II-V-I)

The secret to understanding Jazz is to always look for the progression II - V - I (Subdominant - Dominant - Tonic). In Part A of the standard 'Autumn Leaves', we see how the composer first plays with a II-V-I towards the relative Major key (C Major), and then responds with a II-V-I towards the main Minor key (A Minor).

Chapter 8: Harmonic Minor Scale and its Applications

1. Harmonic Minor Scale

The harmonic minor scale is characterized by its raised seventh degree compared to the natural minor scale, giving it a tighter and more distinctive sound.

Training: T - Major 2nd - Minor 3rd - Just 4th - Just 5th - Minor 6th - Major 7th.

Example in A harmonic minor: A - B - C - D - E - F - G# - A

Differences: In A natural minor, the 7th degree is not raised (G natural instead of G#).

See and Hear Scale

2. Tetrad Chords in the Harmonic Minor Scale

  • I: On(maj7) (A - C - E - G#) - Minor tonic with 7th major.
  • II: Bm7b5 (B - D - F - A) - Subdominant passing chord.
  • III: Cmaj7(#5) (C - E - G# - B) - Ambiguous sound, tends to move to the dominant.
  • IV: Dm7 (D - F - A - C) - Minor subdominant.
  • V: E7 (E - G# - B - D) - Strong dominant that resolves to the tonic minor.
  • VI: Fmaj7 (F - A - C - E) - Subdominant.
  • VII: G#°7 (G# - B - D - F) - Substitute dominant with a lot of tension.

3. Practical Application: Gypsy Jazz

The song "Minor Swing" by Django Reinhardt is the perfect example of the use of the dominant (E7) in a minor key building on the progression of the Gypsy Jazz style.

Am6 ➔ Dm6 ➔ E7 ➔ Am6

To fully understand how Django Reinhardt uses the harmonic minor tension, explore the full harmonic analysis of this piece.
